title: The doors opened (Berakhot 27b–28a)
hookLine: Rabban Gamliel is removed for shaming a student, and the study hall is opened to all
tomorrow: Gamliel has lost his seat. where does he go next?

cards: A screenshot can cross a whole school by lunch. Being embarrassed in front of people is its own kind of hurt, and everyone who watched remembers it. The Talmud has a scene like that.

Rabban Gamliel, head of the academy, hears that Rabbi Joshua disagreed with his ruling. In front of the whole hall he says: Joshua, stand on your feet. Then he keeps teaching, and Joshua stays standing.

teach.b: So, then what? The people in the hall begin to murmur. They stop the lesson.
And they remove Rabban Gamliel from his post, and appoint a young sage, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, in his place.

teach.h: THE GUARD TAKEN FROM THE DOOR.
teach.b: That same day, the Talmud says, the guard at the door was taken away, and students were allowed in. Gamliel had kept a rule: any student whose inside is not like his outside may not enter the study hall.
Now the benches filled, so many that the Talmud records a disagreement over how many were added. And Gamliel, watching the crowd, grew troubled: maybe I kept Torah from people.
Here's the turn worth telling a friend tonight. Shaming one student didn't only hurt one student. It changed who got through the door.
The hall that couldn't hold one man's dignity couldn't hold the crowd either, and when the leader fell, the doors opened.
The Talmud takes public shame seriously elsewhere too: in Bava Metzia, embarrassing someone in public is likened to shedding blood.
And the story isn't finished with Gamliel. He's troubled, which means he's still listening.

how: Jewish law treats embarrassing someone in public as a grave wrong, and synagogues and study halls often open classes to anyone who comes.

o: a rule that students may leave a lesson whenever they like
a study hall opened to all after a leader shamed a student
a holiday when synagogue doors stay open through the night

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: Rabban Gamliel was removed for teaching something wrong
he was removed after making Rabbi Joshua stand in front of everyone.
the day Gamliel was removed, students were let into the study hall

in the Talmud, embarrassing someone in public is a small matter

games.q: you run a study group and only let in people who seem 'serious enough.' after Berakhot 27b–28a, what would you rethink first?
o: the door rule: the day Gamliel fell, the hall opened to everyone.
nothing: the story is only about being polite to your teachers.
the schedule: the sages moved their study to a quieter hour.
games.why: Gamliel's rule kept out students whose inside didn't match their outside. the day he was removed, the guard left the door and benches were added.

practice: Bring to mind one person kept outside something you know: a new kid, a younger cousin, a coworker nobody trains.
Name what they'd want to learn, what's in the way, and the one small door you could open: an invite, an explanation, a saved seat.

wordCard.voice: The doors opened. The day Rabban Gamliel was removed for shaming Rabbi Joshua, the guard left the door and the study hall filled.

orig.note: Hebrew: the study hall, the room whose door was opened that day.

carryVoice: Your line: the doors opened. One student shamed, and a whole hall let in. Sixteen of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 27b–28a (Rabban Gamliel makes Rabbi Joshua stand; he is removed; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah appointed; the doorkeeper removed and benches added)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (shaming another in public likened to shedding blood)
